claims.text: In tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloys, high-temperature plastic-strain capacity is governed by controlled coherent nanoprecipitate formation.
In tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloys, high-temperature toughness is governed by controlled coherent nanoprecipitate formation.
Coherent nanoprecipitates relieve local stress concentrations.
Relieving local stress concentrations delays premature crack initiation.
Coherent nanoprecipitates enhance ductility under extreme high-temperature conditions.
The initial tungsten refractory high-entropy alloy lacks abundant or well-distributed coherent nanoprecipitates.
A stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitation heat-treatment strategy can form coherent nanoprecipitates in a tungsten refractory high-entropy alloy.
The induced coherent nanoprecipitates will be uniformly distributed within the alloy matrix.
Nanoprecipitate coherency and interfacial characteristics promote efficient dislocation transmission.
Nanoprecipitate coherency and interfacial characteristics reduce local stress concentrations.
Relative to an untreated baseline, the SCCP-treated alloy will exhibit greater high-temperature plastic strain.
Relative to an untreated baseline, the SCCP-treated alloy will exhibit a higher work-hardening rate at high temperature.
Relative to an untreated baseline, the SCCP-treated alloy will exhibit superior high-temperature fracture toughness.
Processing without the specialized SCCP heat treatment produces irregular or incoherent nanoscale features.
The proposed mechanism applies over approximately 800–1200 °C in tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloys.
The temperature range of approximately 800–1200 °C is typical of fusion-reactor plasma-facing service conditions.
The optimal precipitate size, spacing, and volume fraction for maximizing the proposed benefits remain uncertain.
